sections.title: The wave that left the headlines

items.q: Where did the 2010s minimalism boom go?
items.a: Matt D'Avella's *Minimalism* streamed **100M+** times and Marie Kondo hit the mainstream — then the cultural headline faded. Ten years on, **consumerism post-COVID** intensified via one-click buying, TikTok/Instagram FOMO, Stanley cups, Labubu, and billionaire weddings.

items.q: Why did minimalism leave the conversation?
items.a: Two reasons: **novelty wore off** (practice continues quietly), and a **polycrisis** — authoritarianism, AI, climate, social media — makes 'too much Amazon' feel secondary as a top worry.

items.q: What does Joshua Fields Millburn say minimalism actually is?
items.a: Not a religion or ideology — a **hammer**: useful personal utility with tangible returns (less cleaning, less mental clutter), not a wrecking ball for institutions. Juliet Schor: a **cultural movement** will never be enough to transform society.

items.q: How do voluntary and forced minimalism differ?
items.a: **Choosing less** while able to afford more is not the same as being **forced into scarcity**. Both respond to unfair outcomes; neither is the root problem of inequality and corporate power.

items.q: What does Juliet Schor argue is the under-discussed driver of spending?
items.a: **Inequality drives consumption**: more equal societies (Japan, much of Europe) show less status spending and debt; the **US is extreme** on both. Robert Frank's **expenditure cascades** ripple from trillionaire excess down to middle-class stretch and lower-income debt for basics.

items.q: How does distress turn into more buying?
items.a: Levi Hildebrand describes a **convenience-culture apathy loop**: when systems feel broken, habitual comfort purchases (Stanley, Starbucks) soothe distress without fixing causes. He cites roughly a **10×** spending spike in a decade, exponential after COVID.

items.q: What two-track policy path does Schor outline?
items.a: Pair **redistribution** (millionaire/billionaire taxes) with fairer **pre-tax market outcomes** — CEO pay limits, unions, antitrust, community power — echoing the post-WWII **great compression** of inequality.

items.q: Is there historical reason for optimism?
items.a: Schor notes crises often precede new structures (**Great Depression → New Deal**). Consumerism is often a **symptom** of other systems going wrong — enough pain eventually triggers 'enough's enough.'
